title: Design a live leaderboard
scopeHtml: Scope: requirements, API, Redis sorted sets, windows, sharding, ties, friends board.

notes.title: Requirements
notes.html:
A live leaderboard shows the top players by score and each player's own rank, updated as scores change. Think of a game ranking (Fortnite, Dream11 contests, Clash of Clans), a coding contest standings board, or a fitness-app weekly challenge. The challenge: ranking millions of players in real time without sorting them on every request.

Functional requirements

  • Submit or update a score for a user.
  • Get the top N (for example top 100) of a leaderboard.
  • Get a user's rank and score, and the players around them (rank +/- 5).
  • Multiple boards: global, per region, per friends, per time window (daily, weekly, all-time).

Non-functional requirements

  • Read p99 under 50 ms; score update visible within 1 s.
  • Scale: 50M players, 20k score updates/s at peak, 100k leaderboard reads/s.
  • Correct ranks (ties handled deterministically); durable scores.
  • Highly available; a stale leaderboard for a few seconds is acceptable.

Decision gravity. Choose an in-memory sorted structure (Redis sorted set) rather than SELECT ... ORDER BY score DESC on a SQL table. SQL needs an index scan and a count to get a rank, O(n) for the count unless carefully indexed, which dies at tens of millions of rows. Redis gives O(log n) for both update and rank. Reversible: the sorted set is a derived view of a durable score table.

Everyday analogy. A scoreboard where cards slide into the correct slot as soon as a team scores, instead of staff re-sorting the whole list every minute.

Common interview traps.

  • Computing rank with COUNT(*) WHERE score > x on every request.
  • Ignoring tie-breaking (two players with 1,000 points).
  • Not saying what happens when Redis loses data.

notes.title: API
notes.html:
POST /v1/boards/global-weekly/scores
Authorization: Bearer <game-server-token>
{ "userId": "u_42", "delta": 150, "eventId": "e_9981" }     // or "score": 8200 for absolute

200 { "userId": "u_42", "score": 8350, "rank": 1204551 }
409 -> duplicate eventId (already applied; returns the existing result)

Server-to-server only: never let clients post their own scores (cheating). eventId makes the update idempotent.

GET /v1/boards/global-weekly/top?limit=100
200 { "updatedAt": "2026-11-09T14:00:02Z",
      "entries": [ { "rank":1, "userId":"u_7", "name":"Neo", "score": 99120 }, ... ] }
GET /v1/boards/global-weekly/users/u_42
200 { "rank": 1204551, "score": 8350, "percentile": 97.6 }

GET /v1/boards/global-weekly/users/u_42/around?span=5
200 { "entries": [ {rank:1204546,...}, ..., {rank:1204556,...} ] }

Friends board: GET /v1/boards/global-weekly/friends?userId=u_42 returns scores of the user's friends (usually a few hundred) sorted by score.

Industry examples. Redis's own documentation uses the leaderboard as the sorted-set showcase; Dream11 and Fortnite-type games rank millions of players in real time; Google Play Games Services exposes a similar leaderboard API.

Everyday analogy. A race marshal who reports your position and the runners just ahead and behind.

Common interview traps.

  • Accepting scores from client apps.
  • Non-idempotent increments, so a retry double-counts.
  • Returning the entire leaderboard instead of a page.

notes.title: Estimates
notes.html:
Assume 50M players on the global board, 20k updates/s peak, 100k reads/s.

Quantity Calculation Result
Sorted-set memory each member ~ 60-100 B (skiplist node + dict entry + 8 B score + id) 50M x ~90 B = ~4.5 GB
Boards global + 30 regions + daily/weekly windows about 100 sets, still < 20 GB
Redis capacity one instance ~ 80-100k simple ops/s; ZADD/ZRANK are O(log n), ~20 comparisons at 50M 20k writes + 100k reads needs read replicas
Top-N response 100 entries x 60 B 6 KB, cacheable
Durable store 50M rows x 100 B per board ~5 GB per board
Write log 20k/s x 100 B 2 MB/s = 170 GB/day (retain 7 days in Kafka)

Memory is modest, so a single Redis shard can hold the whole board; the pressure is op rate and fault tolerance, not size.

Industry example. Redis sorted sets store ~10M-member sets comfortably in a few GB; teams report millisecond ZRANK on tens of millions.

Everyday analogy. The whole scoreboard fits on one wall; the issue is how many people are reading it at once.

Common interview traps.

  • Sharding at 5 GB when one node suffices.
  • Forgetting that 100k reads/s must be spread across replicas.
  • Counting only storage and not op rate.

notes.title: High-level design
notes.html:
Components:

  • Score service: authenticates the game server, validates (max delta per event), dedupes by eventId (Redis SET NX with 24 h TTL), publishes to Kafka.
  • Kafka, partitioned by userId, preserves per-user order.
  • Ranking updater: applies ZINCRBY board userId delta (or ZADD GT for best-score boards) to Redis.
  • Redis primary + 2 replicas per board shard; reads go to replicas.
  • Persister: writes the durable score table (source of truth) and snapshots.
  • Top-N cache: top 100 recomputed every 1 s and cached in the app (it changes slowly at the top).
  • Profile service: joins userId to display name and avatar at read time.

Decision gravity: Redis as derived, not primary. Why: durable table plus Kafka allows rebuilding the sorted set (ZADD bulk load of 50M takes a few minutes). Alternative: Redis as the only store with AOF; faster to build but riskier. Breaks if a failover loses recent writes; replay the last minutes from Kafka. Reversible.

Decision gravity: tie-breaking. Redis orders equal scores lexicographically by member, which is arbitrary. For "first to reach the score wins", encode score * 2^20 + (MAX_TS - timestamp) into a double (careful: a double has 53 bits of integer precision). That choice is a one-way door for existing data because all stored scores change shape; decide before launch.

Industry examples. Riot, Supercell and Zynga have described leaderboards built on Redis; Discord-like bots use ZSETs; large sites often combine Redis with SQL for durability.

Everyday analogy. The scoreboard operator (Redis) works from the official scorer's sheets (SQL); if the board is wiped he can redo it from the sheets.

Common interview traps.

  • Not choosing a tie-breaker.
  • Floating-point precision for composite scores.
  • Reading names from Redis (keep it lean; fetch profile data elsewhere).

notes.title: Deep dives
notes.html:
How the sorted set works

A Redis ZSET is a skiplist (ordered by score) plus a hash table (member to score). ZADD and ZRANK are O(log n); ZREVRANGE 0 99 is O(log n + 100). Rank is derived from skiplist span counters, no scan.

ZADD lb:global:2026w45 GT 8350 u_42
ZREVRANK lb:global:2026w45 u_42            # 0-based rank from top
ZREVRANGE lb:global:2026w45 0 99 WITHSCORES
ZREVRANGE lb:global:2026w45 1204546 1204556 WITHSCORES   # around me

Time windows

Keys like lb:global:d:2026-11-09 with EXPIRE of 8 days; weekly sets expire after the following week. At window end snapshot the top 1,000 to SQL for history and rewards. Writing to 3 keys triples write ops (60k/s): still fine for a pipeline of batched commands.

Scaling past one node

When a single set no longer fits or ops exceed limits (hundreds of millions of members, 100k+ writes/s), shard.

Option A, partition by userId hash: updates scale, but global top-N needs merging the top N from each shard (cheap: N x shards) and exact rank needs summing counts across shards (ZCOUNT on each: expensive). Option B, partition by score range: exact rank is sum of sizes of higher shards + local rank, but hot ranges cause imbalance and users migrate shards as scores grow. Pragmatic answer: hash shard plus approximate rank for deep positions ("top 3%") and exact rank only for the top 10,000. Decision gravity: sharding scheme is a one-way door.

Approximate rank at huge scale

Maintain a histogram of scores (for example 1,000 buckets updated with counters). Rank of a score = sum of counts in higher buckets plus interpolation. Error stays under 0.1%, cost O(buckets). Used when nobody cares whether you are 1,204,551st or 1,204,600th.

Friends leaderboard

Friend lists are small (under a few thousand): fetch the friend ids, ZMSCORE/pipelined ZSCORE for each, sort in the service. Alternative: store a per-user friends ZSET (fan-out on write, expensive for large graphs). Compute on read with a 5-10 s cache.

Hot reads and consistency

Top 100 is read by everyone: cache in app memory with 1 s TTL (100k reads/s become 1 per second per server). Own-rank read goes to a replica; replication lag of tens of ms means a player might not see their just-submitted score; read-your-writes by returning the new score and rank in the POST response and showing it directly.

Persistence and recovery

Source of truth: scores(board, user_id, score, updated_at) in Postgres/Cassandra, written from Kafka consumers. Redis with AOF everysec plus replicas; on total loss rebuild from the table in minutes. Idempotent eventId prevents double counts during replay.

Anti-cheat

Server-authoritative scores only, cap per-event delta, anomaly detection (score jump rate), and a shadow-ban list excluded from top-N queries.

Production incident patterns. (1) Redis memory growth because old window keys never expire: metric used_memory, check keys without TTL. (2) A big ZREVRANGE 0 -1 blocks the single-threaded Redis; enforce a max page size of 100-1000 and use SLOWLOG. (3) Failover loses the last second of writes; compare Redis against Kafka offsets, replay.

Industry examples. Redis sorted sets, Dream11 contests, Fortnite rankings, and Codeforces-like standings for contests.

Everyday analogy. Sorting a class by marks: keep a sorted list and slot each new mark in, rather than re-sorting the whole class for each question.

Common interview traps.

  • Thinking sharding is mandatory at 50M members.
  • Exact global rank across hash shards without saying the cost.
  • Letting clients submit scores.

notes.title: What interviewers look for
notes.html:
• Choosing a sorted structure and explaining O(log n) rank and update.
  • Sizing: 50M members is only a few GB.
  • Durability story: SQL/Kafka as source of truth, Redis as a rebuildable view.
  • Windows, friends boards and tie-breaking handled explicitly.
  • Hot-read caching of top N, replicas for reads.
  • A believable scale-out path (hash shards plus approximations) and its trade-offs.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Redis sorted set: ZINCRBY/ZADD for updates, ZREVRANK for rank, ZREVRANGE for top N, all O(log n).
  • 50M members is about 4.5 GB; one primary with replicas covers 20k writes/s and 100k reads/s.
  • Scores come from trusted servers with idempotent event ids; Kafka feeds Redis and the durable table.
  • Separate keys per window (daily, weekly) with TTLs; snapshot winners to SQL.
  • Cache the top 100 for 1 s; neighbours via rank +/- span.
  • Shard only when forced, using approximate ranks for deep positions.
  • Pick the tie-break encoding before launch; it is hard to change later.

questions.promptHtml: You are asked to build a live leaderboard for 50M players. Why not just run SELECT ... ORDER BY score DESC LIMIT 100 and COUNT(*) WHERE score > x against a SQL table?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It separates people who know rank is an order-statistic problem from people who reach for a table by habit.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Rank means "how many players have a higher score", and in SQL that is a range count over millions of rows per request. Even with an index it is O(n) in the worst case, and at 100k reads/s it dies. A Redis sorted set keeps members ordered in a skiplist with span counters, so update and rank are both O(log n), around 20 comparisons for 50M members. I keep SQL as the durable source of truth and treat Redis as a rebuildable view.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A B-tree index gives ordered iteration, but a plain B-tree does not store subtree counts, so "position of this key" needs a scan of everything above it. A skiplist stores how many nodes each forward pointer skips, so the rank is the sum of spans on the search path.

ZSET = hash(member -> score)  +  skiplist ordered by (score, member)
ZADD / ZINCRBY      O(log n)
ZREVRANK            O(log n)   (sum of span counters on the path)
ZREVRANGE 0 99      O(log n + 100)

Memory: about 90 B per member, so 50M members is about 4.5 GB. It fits on one box; the pressure is ops/s, not size.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
the four commands you need.

ZADD lb:global:2026w45 GT 8350 u_42
ZREVRANK lb:global:2026w45 u_42
ZREVRANGE lb:global:2026w45 0 99 WITHSCORES
ZREVRANGE lb:global:2026w45 1204546 1204556 WITHSCORES

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Computing rank with COUNT(*) WHERE score > x per request.
  • Treating Redis as the only copy of scores.
  • Sharding at 5 GB when one node already holds the data.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is SQL ever fine? -> Yes under about 100k players or a nightly-refreshed board; an indexed count is simpler and fast enough.
  2. What does ZREVRANK return for the top player? -> 0, it is zero-based, so add 1 for display.
  3. Could a Postgres materialised view do it? -> Refresh cost and staleness make it a batch answer, not a live one.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer says "Redis is fast". The senior names the structure (skiplist with spans), the complexity, the memory estimate, and the durability split.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams that started with COUNT(*) ranks hit a wall when contest traffic arrived and moved ranks into Redis with the DB as ledger.

questions.promptHtml: Two players both have 1,000 points. Who is ranked higher in Redis, and how do you make "first to reach the score wins" deterministic?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Ties are the classic forgotten requirement, and the fix hides a floating-point precision trap.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Redis orders equal scores by member string, lexicographically, which is arbitrary for users. To get "earlier wins" I encode a composite score: points * 2^20 + (WINDOW - secondsSinceStart), so an earlier time gives a bigger low part. Scores are doubles with 53 bits of exact integer precision, so the points part gets at most 33 bits (about 8.6 billion). I must decide this before launch because every stored score changes shape.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A double represents integers exactly up to 2^53. If the time part uses 20 bits (604,800 seconds of a week fits in 2^20), the points part has 33 bits left. Exceed that and low bits are silently rounded, so ties come back.

composite = points * 2^20 + (WINDOW_SECONDS - secondsSinceWindowStart)
points    = floor(composite / 2^20)

For a never-ending all-time board a time tie-break needs another scheme (for example a hash with first-reached time, resolved at read time).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
static double encode(long points, long secondsSinceStart, long windowSeconds) {
    if (points >= (1L << 33)) throw new IllegalArgumentException("precision");
    return (double) ((points << 20) + (windowSeconds - secondsSinceStart));
}
fun encode(points: Long, secondsSinceStart: Long, windowSeconds: Long): Double {
    require(points < (1L shl 33)) { "precision" }
    return ((points shl 20) + (windowSeconds - secondsSinceStart)).toDouble()
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using epoch milliseconds in the low bits and blowing the 53-bit budget.
  • Showing the composite score to users instead of decoding it.
  • Changing the encoding after launch without rewriting all sets.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What about ZINCRBY with composite scores? -> Increments must add delta << 20 and set the time part to the latest improvement time, so use a Lua script or recompute from the durable table.
  2. Dense ranks (1,2,2,3)? -> Compute at read time from distinct decoded points; Redis rank is positional.
  3. Why not a separate hash for time? -> Fine for display, but ordering needs it inside the score.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "sort by timestamp second". Senior: the bit budget, the one-way-door nature of the encoding, and the all-time-board limitation.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A tournament shipped with arbitrary tie order; support tickets about prize splits forced a re-encode and rebuild.

questions.contextHtml:
Daily and weekly boards use keys lb:global:d:<date> and lb:global:w:<week>. Redis used_memory rose from 6 GB to 21 GB over three weeks and the box is at 85 percent of maxmemory with noeviction. Write errors (OOM command not allowed) have started for the score updater. A recent change moved window rollover into a nightly cron.

127.0.0.1:6379> INFO memory
used_memory_human:20.9G   maxmemory_human:24G
127.0.0.1:6379> DBSIZE
(integer) 41
127.0.0.1:6379> TTL lb:global:d:2026-10-20
(integer) -1

Traffic and QPS are unchanged. The team suspects a memory leak in the client library.
questions.promptHtml: What is happening and how do you fix it without losing live data?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Upgrade Redis or add memory." It treats a lifecycle bug as a capacity problem and never looks at TTL on the keys.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which job sets EXPIRE and when? Do we still need old daily boards (history lives in SQL snapshots)? What is the eviction policy and is there an alert on used_memory?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Confirm the top-1000 snapshot exists in SQL, then UNLINK daily keys older than 8 days (about 4.5 GB per global set). UNLINK frees asynchronously.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) the cron that sets EXPIRE failed or never ran; (b) EXPIRE applied only on creation and a later DEL/rename cleared it; (c) key name changed so cleanup patterns miss; (d) a client leak (least likely: DBSIZE is only 41 keys).
  4. How I'd verify each: redis-cli --scan --pattern 'lb:*' then TTL and MEMORY USAGE per key. A few huge keys with TTL -1 confirms (a) or (b). Check cron logs.
  5. Root cause: Old window keys were never given a TTL; each is a full multi-GB set. Key count is tiny, so DBSIZE hid the problem (red herring: client leak).
  6. Fix: Short term, snapshot and UNLINK. Long term, set expiry atomically with the write path: pipeline ZINCRBY plus EXPIRE key 691200 NX (Redis 7 option; verify your version) or a Lua script, instead of a separate cron.
  7. Prevention: Alert on keys without TTL (sampled scan) and on used_memory slope; a test asserting every window key has a TTL.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not switch to allkeys-lru: it could evict the live board. I would not FLUSHALL.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the snapshot job failed too? -> Rebuild the day from the durable score table before deleting.
  • Why UNLINK over DEL? -> DEL of a multi-GB set blocks the single thread; UNLINK frees in a background thread.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A weekly contest board lived for a year because expiry was set by a cron that silently started failing. Memory drifted up slowly and the page came at 3 a.m. when the primary hit maxmemory.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Adds memory or blames the client.
  • Hire: Finds missing TTL and fixes with UNLINK and atomic EXPIRE.
  • Strong hire: Adds alerting on TTL-less keys, history snapshots, and avoids LRU eviction hazards.

questions.contextHtml: The board runs on one Redis primary with two replicas: 50M members, 20k writes/s, 100k reads/s. A new game launches and the plan says 500M members, 200k score updates/s and 1M reads/s at peak. Every update writes three keys (daily, weekly, all-time). Read p99 SLO is 50 ms.
questions.promptHtml: Does it still fit on one primary? What do you change, and what do you refuse to promise?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Shard by userId" without numbers, or "just add replicas" for write load.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is 500M members on one board or across boards? Is exact global rank required for everyone? How many reads are top-N versus own-rank?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; first the math. Memory: 500M x 90 B = 45 GB for the all-time set, similar for weekly. Possible on a big node but risky for fork and failover time.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: The binding limit is writes: 200k x 3 = 600k writes/s, far above roughly 100k ops/s per primary thread. Reads at 1M/s can go to replicas plus an app cache.
  4. How I'd verify each: Load test one shard with redis-benchmark and pipelined ZADD; watch instantaneous_ops_per_sec and BGSAVE fork time on a 45 GB heap.
  5. Root cause: Single-threaded command execution caps writes per primary; replicas scale only reads.
  6. Fix: Hash-shard by userId across 8 to 16 primaries (600k / ~60k each) with pipelined writes. Top-N: each shard returns its top 100, an aggregator merges 16 x 100 entries and caches 1 s. Own rank: exact for the top 10,000 (merged), histogram-approximate for the rest ("top 3 percent").
  7. Prevention: Per-shard ops/s and memory dashboards, a resharding runbook, a game day for a lost shard.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not promise exact rank for position 213,000,001: it costs a ZCOUNT fan-out per request. Sharding is a one-way door, so I would use many virtual slots (for example 256) up front.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if product insists on exact rank? -> Range-partition by score; rank = sizes of higher shards + local rank, accepting hot ranges and migrations.
  • Can we drop the all-time write? -> Yes if it is derived hourly from the durable table.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team sharded at 5 GB because the memory "felt big", then paid a year of merge complexity for what was really an ops/s problem at 10x.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Replicas for writes, or no numbers.
  • Hire: Computes 600k writes/s, hash shards, merged top-N.
  • Strong hire: Adds approximate rank, virtual shards as one-way door, and a per-shard failure plan.

questions.contextHtml:
The Redis primary crashed at 14:00:00 and a replica was promoted at 14:00:09. Players complain their scores from the last few seconds are missing. The replica was about 1.2 MB behind at the crash; Kafka consumer group ranking-updater is current; the durable scores table is current.

role:master  (promoted)
ranking-updater: lag 0 (committed offset 8,812,400)

On-call proposes "replay the last 30 seconds from Kafka with ZINCRBY".
questions.promptHtml: Is that replay safe, and how do you repair the board?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Replaying deltas blindly and double counting every event the replica did receive.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are events deltas or absolutes? Is eventId dedupe state (Redis SET NX) on the same lost primary? How stale is the persister?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Keep serving; a few seconds of staleness is in the SLO. Show the score returned by the POST so players see their own value.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Async replication lost the last ~1 s of ZINCRBY; dedupe keys were lost too, so a naive replay could count twice.
  4. How I'd verify each: Compare ZSCORE against the scores table for users updated in the last 30 s and count mismatches.
  5. Root cause: Redis replication is asynchronous; promotion dropped an unreplicated tail.
  6. Fix: Repair idempotently: collect userIds touched in the last 60 s from Kafka, read their authoritative scores from the durable store, and ZADD absolute values (replace, never increment). Then resume the updater.
  7. Prevention: The durable table is the repair authority; track Redis-vs-SQL drift as a metric; WAIT only for high-value writes.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not replay ZINCRBY without a dedupe store, and I would not make 20k writes/s synchronous.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the persister lags more than Redis? -> Replay Kafka into the table first, then repair from the table.
  • Why not AOF always? -> Heavy fsync cost; a rebuildable view does not need it.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: After a failover a replay doubled the scores of 40k players in a prize round. The fix was an absolute rewrite from the ledger and a rule: repairs are idempotent, never additive.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Replays increments.
  • Hire: Reconciles from the durable table with ZADD.
  • Strong hire: Explains lost dedupe state, drift metric, and where synchronous writes would be justified.

questions.contextHtml:
At 20:10 leaderboard read p99 jumps from 12 ms to 6 s for about 8 seconds, then recovers, and repeats every few minutes. One Redis core is at 100 percent. App servers are healthy; the network team says bandwidth is normal. A data scientist's export notebook has read access to production Redis.

127.0.0.1:6379> SLOWLOG GET 1
1) 1) (integer) 412
   2) (integer) 1731182461
   3) (integer) 5910342          # microseconds
   4) 1) "ZREVRANGE" 2) "lb:global:w:2026-45" 3) "0" 4) "-1" 5) "WITHSCORES"
   5) "10.2.3.77:52114"
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose, stop it, and prevent a repeat.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Blames the network or scales app servers, missing that one command blocks the single-threaded server.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which client is 10.2.3.77? Is the API the only reader? Do replicas stall too?
  2. Immediate mitigation: CLIENT KILL ADDR 10.2.3.77:52114 and block the host; the stall stops because the command runs on the main thread.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) full-range read by the notebook; (b) a KEYS * scan; (c) BGSAVE fork pause; (d) network saturation.
  4. How I'd verify each: SLOWLOG GET, LATENCY DOCTOR, INFO commandstats (usec per call for zrevrange), CLIENT LIST. The 5.9 s entry matches the stall windows; fork and bandwidth show nothing.
  5. Root cause: ZREVRANGE 0 -1 WITHSCORES returns 50M entries (about 1 GB) serialised on the one thread, blocking every other command.
  6. Fix: ACL users: the notebook gets a read-only user on an analytics replica without @dangerous and @slow categories; the API enforces limit <= 100; exports run from the SQL source of truth.
  7. Prevention: Alerts on slowlog, command-level ACLs, no ad hoc access to production Redis.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not just raise timeouts, and I would not rely on a wiki rule.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the API itself allows limit=100000? -> Cap at 100-1000 and bound offsets.
  • Could io-threads help? -> They parallelise network I/O, not command execution; the big range still blocks.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: An unbounded range cell in a notebook ran every 5 minutes; the symptoms looked like GC pauses in the app for two days.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Network or app scaling.
  • Hire: Finds the SLOWLOG entry and caps page size.
  • Strong hire: ACL separation, analytics replica, slow-command alerting.

questions.contextHtml: A contest app ranks 50M players with Postgres: scores(user_id, score, updated_at) with an index on score. Rank queries (SELECT count(*) FROM scores WHERE score > $1) take 1.5 s and the DB is at 70 percent CPU at 3k rank reads/s. You must move ranks to Redis with zero downtime during a live season, and there is no event log today.
questions.promptHtml: Lay out the migration, the cutover and the rollback.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Export, import, switch on Sunday night." No consistency check, no rollback.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is score only incremented or also reset? How many writers exist? Can I accept a few seconds of read-only?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cache top-100 for 1 s now to cut DB load while I build.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Risks: losing writes between bulk load and cutover; Redis disagreeing with SQL; tie semantics changing.
  4. How I'd verify each: Shadow comparison of ranks for a 10k-user sample, tolerating ties.
  5. Root cause: Not an incident; the structural problem is rank by count.
  6. Fix (plan): (1) Publish every score change to Kafka (or CDC via logical decoding). (2) Start the Redis updater consuming from now. (3) Bulk load the 50M existing scores with ZADD absolute values in pipelines of 10k; events after the snapshot time are applied after. (4) Shadow reads: API computes both, returns SQL, logs mismatch rate. (5) Canary 1 percent of reads, then 100 percent. (6) SQL stays source of truth.
  7. Prevention: Drift dashboard, a periodic repair from SQL for recent updates, a rebuild runbook.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Rollback is a flag back to SQL reads; I keep SQL rank code for two clean weeks. I would not dual-write from the client.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Tie order differs from SQL? -> Fix the tie encoding before the bulk load and document it.
  • Bulk load too slow? -> Parallel pipelined connections; still minutes for 50M.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A migration without shadow reads went live with ranks off by one for every tied player; a mismatch metric would have caught it in an hour.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Big-bang export/import.
  • Hire: Snapshot plus catch-up plus flagged cutover.
  • Strong hire: Shadow reads, absolute writes, rollback, tie semantics.

questions.contextHtml:
Postmortem: for 40 minutes 9 accounts held ranks 1-9 with scores near 4 million, where the previous top was 99,120. The score API accepted delta values up to 450,000 from one game-server token. The eventId dedupe blocked replays but each call used a fresh id. A client mod had found a leaked staging token still accepted in production. Paid rewards are distributed at week end.

POST /v1/boards/global-weekly/scores  token=gs-staging-01  delta=450000  eventId=e_aa1...
200 {"score": 3998020, "rank": 1}
questions.promptHtml: Run the review: what failed, how do you repair the board, and what changes?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add rate limiting" only, with no repair and no look at token scope.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which tokens exist per environment? Is every event stored with its writer? When are rewards cut?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Revoke the token, shadow-ban the 9 users (excluded from top-N reads), freeze reward calculation.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Leaked unscoped credential; no per-event cap; no velocity anomaly detector; production accepting a staging token.
  4. How I'd verify each: Query the events table by token and delta distribution; p99 delta is about 300, the attack used 450,000.
  5. Root cause: Authentication was valid but authorisation too broad, with no server-side sanity bound.
  6. Fix: Rebuild affected users from events excluding the tainted token (ZADD absolute), then unfreeze. Add max delta per event and per user per minute, per-environment token audiences and a velocity alert. Scores stay server-authoritative.
  7. Prevention: Short-lived signed tokens, secret scanning, rewards delayed 24 h behind a review job.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not delete accounts without evidence; shadow-banning keeps the investigation reversible.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Cheaters spread many small deltas under the cap? -> Statistical anomaly detection on score rate versus play time, plus game telemetry.
  • Why not harden duplicate rejection? -> eventId solves retries, not forged events.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A tournament paid out before review; the clawback cost more than the anti-cheat project would have.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Rate limiting only.
  • Hire: Revokes, caps delta, rebuilds from events.
  • Strong hire: Separates retries from forgery, delays rewards, scopes tokens, adds velocity analytics.
